Afflictive; as sour adversities. [Not in use.] NWAD SOUR.5
Expressing discontent or peevishness. He never uttered a sour word. The lord treasurer often looked on me with a sour countenance. NWAD SOUR.6
Harsh to the feelings; cold and damp; as sour weather. NWAD SOUR.7
Turned, as milk; coagulated. NWAD SOUR.9
To make acid; to cause to have a sharp taste. So the sun\'s heat, with different pow\'rs, ripens the grape, the liquor sours. NWAD SOUR.12
To make harsh, cold or unkindly. Tufts of grass sour land. NWAD SOUR.13
To make harsh in temper; to make cross, crabbed, peevish or discontented. Misfortunes often sour\'d, nor wrath debas\'d my heart. NWAD SOUR.14
To make uneasy or less agreeable. Hail, great king! To sour your happiness I must report the queen is dead. NWAD SOUR.15
In rural economy, to macerate, as lime, and render fir for plaster or mortar. NWAD SOUR.16

To become acid; to acquire the quality of tartness or pungency to the taste. Cider sours rapidly in the rays of the sun. When food sours in the stomach, it is evidence of imperfect digestion. NWAD SOUR.18
TO become peevish or crabbed. They hinder the hatred of vice from souring into severity. NWAD SOUR.19
SOURCE: Properly, the spring or fountain from which a stream of water proceeds, or any collection of water within the earth or upon its surface, in which a stream originates. This is called also the head of the stream. We call the water of a spring, where it issues from the earth, the source of the stream or rivulet proceeding form it. We say also that springs have their sources in subterranean ponds, lakes or collections of water. We say also that a large river has is source in a lake. For example, the St. Lawrence has its source in the great lakes of America. NWAD SOURCE.2

First cause; original; that which gives rise to any thing. Thus ambition, the love of power and of fame, have been the sources of half the calamities of nations. Intemperance is the source of innumerable evils to individuals. NWAD SOURCE.3
The first producer; he or that which originates; as Greece the source of arts. NWAD SOURCE.4
SOURDET: n. The little pipe of a trumpet.
SOUR-GOURD: n. A plant of the genus Adansonia.
SOURING: ppr. Making acid; becoming sour; making peevish.
SOURISH: a. Somewhat sour; moderately acid; as sourish fruit; a sourish taste.
SOURLY: With peevishness; with acrimony. The stern Athenian prince the sourly smil\'d. NWAD SOURLY.3
SOURNESS: Acidity; sharpness to the taste; tartness; as the sourness of vinegar or of fruit. Sourness being one of those simple ideas which one cannot describe. NWAD SOURNESS.2
Asperity; harshness of temper. Take care that no sourness and moroseness mingle with our seriousness of mind. NWAD SOURNESS.3
SOUR-SOP: n. A plant, the annona muricata. The custard apple.
SOUS: n. plu. of sou or sol. [See Sou .]
SOUSE: Pickle made with salt. NWAD SOUSE.2
Something kept or steeped on pickle. NWAD SOUSE.3
The ears, feet, etc. of swine. [America.] NWAD SOUSE.4
To steep in pickle. But souse the cabbage with a bounteous heart. NWAD SOUSE.6
To plunge into water. They soused me into the Thames, with as little remorse as they drown blind puppies. NWAD SOUSE.7

v.i. [See Soss . This word is probably the same as the preceding, to plunge, to dip; I believe from the Armoric.] To fall suddenly on; to rush with speed; as a hawk on its prey. Jove\'s bird will souse upon the tim\'rous hare.
v.t. To strike with sudden violence.
adv. With sudden violence. [This word is low and vulgar.]
SOUTER: n. [L. sutor.] A shoemaker; a cobler. [Not in use.]
SOUTERLY: adv. Like a cobler. [Not in use.]
SOUTERRAIN: n. A grotto or cavern under ground. [Not English.]
SOUTH: The north and south are opposite points in the horizon; each ninety degrees or the quarter of a great circle distant from the east and west. A man standing with his face towards the east or rising sun, has the south on his right hand. The meridian of every place is a great circle passing through the north and south points. Strictly, south is the horizontal point in the meridian of a place, on the right hand of a person standing with his face towards the east. But the word is applied to any point in the meridian, between the horizon and the zenith. NWAD SOUTH.2
In a less exact sense, any point or place on the earth or in the heavens, which is near the meridian towards the right hand as one faces the east. NWAD SOUTH.3

A southern region, country or place; as the queen of the south, in Scriptures. So in Europe, the people of Spain and Italy are spoken of as living in the south. In the United States, we speak of the states of the south, and of the north. NWAD SOUTH.4
The wind that blows from the north. [Not used.] NWAD SOUTH.5
In any place north of the tropic of Cancer, pertaining to or lying in the meridian towards the sun; as a south wind. NWAD SOUTH.7
Being in a southern direction; as the south sea. NWAD SOUTH.8
adv. Towards the south. A ship sails south; the wind blows south.
SOUTHEAST: n. The point of the compass equally distant from the south and east.
a. In the direction of southeast, or coming from the southeast; s a southeast wind.
SOUTHERLY: Lying at the south, or in a direction nearly south; as a southerly point. NWAD SOUTHERLY.2
Coming from the south or a point nearly south; as a southerly wind. NWAD SOUTHERLY.3
SOUTHERN: Belonging to the south; meridional; as the southern hemisphere. NWAD SOUTHERN.2
Lying towards the south; as a southern country or climate. NWAD SOUTHERN.3
Coming form the south; as a southern breeze. NWAD SOUTHERN.4
SOUTHERNMOST: a. suth\'ernmost. Furthest towards the south.
SOTHERNWOOD: n. suth\'ernwood, A plant agreeing in most parts with the wormwood. The southernwood is the Artemisia abrotanum, a different species form the wormwood.
SOUTHING: a. Going towards the south; as the southing sun.
Tendency or motion to the south. NWAD SOUTHING.3
The southing of the moon, the time at which the moon passes the meridian. NWAD SOUTHING.4
Course or distance south; as a ship\'s southing. NWAD SOUTHING.5
SOUTHWARD: adv. suth\'ard. Towards the south; as, to go southward.
n. suth\'ard. The southern regions or countries.
SOUTHWEST: n. [south and west.] The point of the compass equally distant from the south and west.
Lying in the direction of the southwest; as a southwest country. NWAD SOUTHWEST.3
Coming from the southwest; as a southwest wind. NWAD SOUTHWEST.4
SOUTHWESTERLY: In the direction of southwest, or nearly so. NWAD SOUTHWESTERLY.2
Coming from the southwest, or a point near it; as a southwesterly wind. NWAD SOUTHWESTERLY.3
SOUTHWESTERN: In the direction of southwest, or nearly so; as, to sail a southwestern course.
SOVENANCE: n. Remembrance. [Not English, nor it used.]
SOVEREIGN: a. suv\'eran. [We retain this babarous orthography from the Norman sovereign. The true spelling would be suveran from the L. supernes, superus.]
Supreme in power; possessing supreme dominion; as a sovereign ruler of the universe. NWAD SOVEREIGN.2
Supreme; superior to all others; chief. God is the sovereign good of all who love and obey him. NWAD SOVEREIGN.3
Supremely efficacious; superior to all others; predominant; effectual; as a sovereign remedy. NWAD SOVEREIGN.4
Supreme; pertaining to the first magistrate of a nation; as sovereign authority. NWAD SOVEREIGN.5
A supreme lord or ruler; one who possesses the highest authority without control. Some earthly princes, kings and emperors are sovereigns in their dominions. NWAD SOVEREIGN.7
A supreme magistrate; a king. NWAD SOVEREIGN.8
A gold coin of England, value 20s or $4.44 NWAD SOVEREIGN.9
SOVEREIGNIZE: v.i. suv\'eranize. To exercise supreme authority. [Not in use.]
SOVEREIGNLY: adv. suv\'eranly. Supreme power; supremacy; the possession power. Absolute sovereignty belongs to God only.
SOW: The female of the hog kind or of swine. NWAD SOW.2
An oblong piece of lead. NWAD SOW.3
An insect; a milleped. NWAD SOW.4
v.t. pret. sowed; pp. sowed or sown. [L. sevi. This word is probably contracted.]

To scatter on ground, for the purpose growth and the production of a crop; as, to sow good seed; to sow a bushel of wheat or rye to the acre; to sow oats, clover or barley; to sow seed in drills, or to sow it broad cast. Oats and flax should be sown early in the spring. NWAD SOW.2
To scatter seed over for growth; as, to sow ground or land; to sow ten or a hundred acres in a year. NWAD SOW.3
To spread or to originate; to propagate; as, to sow discord. Born to afflict my Marcia\'s family, and sow dissension in the hearts of brothers. NWAD SOW.4
To supply or stock with seed. The intellectual faculty is a goodly field, and it is the worst husbandry in the world to sow it with trifles. NWAD SOW.5
To scatter over; to besprinkle. He sow\'d with stars the heaven. Morn now sow\'d the earth with orient pearl. NWAD SOW.6
v.i. To scatter seed for growth and the production of a crop. In New England, farmers begin to sow in April. They that sow in tears, shall reap in joy. Psalm 126:5 .
for sew, is not in use. [See Sew .]
SOW-BREAD: n. A plant of the genus Cyclamen.
SOW-THISTLE: n. A plant of the genus Sonchus. The downy sow-thistle is of the genus Andryala.
SOWED: pp. Scattered on ground, as seed; sprinkled with seed, as ground. We say, seed is sowed; or land is sowed.
SOWER: He that scatters seed for propagation. Behold, a sower went forth to sow. Matthew 13:3 . NWAD SOWER.2
One who scatters or spreads; as a sower of words. NWAD SOWER.3
A breeder; a promoter; as a sower of suits. NWAD SOWER.4
SOWING: ppr. Scattering, as seed; sprinkling with seed, as ground; stocking with seed.
n. The act of scattering seed for propagation.
SOWINS: n. Flummery made of oatmeal somewhat soured. [Not used. I believe, in America.]
SOWN: pp. Scattered, as seed; sprinkled with seed, as ground.
SOY: n. A kind of source, used in Japan.
SOZZLE: n. [See Soss .] A sluttish woman, or one that spills water and other liquids carelessly. [New England.]
SPAAD: n. A kind of mineral; spar.
SPACE: n. [L. spatium, space; spatior, to wander. This word is probably formed on the root of pateo.]
Room; extension. Space in the abstract, is mere extension. Pure space is capable neither of resistance nor motion. NWAD SPACE.2

Any quantity of extension. In relation to bodies, space is the interval between any two or more object\' as the space between two stars or two hills The quantity of space or extent between bodies, constitutes their distance form each other. NWAD SPACE.3
The distance or interval between lines; as in books. The space in music are named as well as the lines. NWAD SPACE.4

Quantity of time; also, the interval between two points of time. Nine times the space that measures day and God may defer his judgment for a time, and give a people a longer space for repentance. NWAD SPACE.5
A short time; a while. To stay your deadly strife a space. [This sense is nearly obsolete.] NWAD SPACE.6
v.t. Among printers, to make space or wider intervals between lines.
SPACIOUS: Wide; roomy; having large or ample room; not narrow; as a spacious church; a spacious hall or drawing room. NWAD SPACIOUS.2
Extensive; vast in extent; as the spacious earth; the spacious ocean. NWAD SPACIOUS.3
SPACIOUSNESS: Wideness; largeness of extent; roominess; as the spaciousness of the rooms in a building. NWAD SPACIOUSNESS.2
Extensiveness; vastness of extent; as the spaciousness of the ocean. NWAD SPACIOUSNESS.3
SPADDLE: n. [dim of spade.] A little spade.
SPADE: n. [L. spatula, from the root of pateo.]
An instrument for digging, consisting of a broad palm with a handle. NWAD SPADE.2
A suit of cards. NWAD SPADE.3
A deer three years old; written also spaid. NWAD SPADE.4
A gelded beast. [L. spado.] NWAD SPADE.5
SPADE-BONE: n. [spade and bone.] The shoulder blade. [I believe little used.]
SPADEFUL: n. [spade and full.] As much as a spade will hold.
SPADICEOUS: a. [L. spadiceus, from spadix, a light red color.]
Of a light red color, usually denominated bay. NWAD SPADICEOUS.2
In botany, a spadiceous flower, is a sort of aggregate flower, having a receptacle common to many florets, within a spathe, as in palms, dracontium, arum, etc. NWAD SPADICEOUS.3
SPADILLE: n. spadil\'. The ace of spades at omber.
SPADIX: n. [L.] In botany, the receptacle in palms and some other plants, proceeding from a spathe.
SPAHEE: n. [See Seapoy .] One of the Turkish cavalry.
SPAHI: n. [See Seapoy .] One of the Turkish cavalry.
SPAKE: pret. of speak; nearly obsolete. We not use spoke.
SPALT: n. A whitish scaly mineral, used to promote the fusion of metals.
n. A species of grain of the genus Triticum; called also German wheat.
SPELT: n. A whitish scaly mineral, used to promote the fusion of metals.
n. A species of grain of the genus Triticum; called also German wheat.
SPAN: n. [This word is formed on the root of bend, L. pando. The primary sense is to strain, stretch, extend, hence to join a team.]
The space from the end of the thumb to the end of the little finger when extended; nine inches; the eighth of a fathom. NWAD SPAN.2
A short space of time. Life\'s but a span; I\'ll every inch enjoy. NWAD SPAN.3

A span of horses, consists of two of nearly the same color, and otherwise nearly alike, which are usually harness side by side. The word signifies properly the same as yoke, when applied to horned cattle, from buckling or fastening together. But in America, span always implies resemblance in color at least; it being an object of ambition with gentlemen and with teamters to unite two horses abreast that are alike. NWAD SPAN.4
In seamen\'s language, a small line or cord, the middle of which is attached to a stay. NWAD SPAN.5
To measure by the hand with the fingers extended, or with the fingers encompassing the object; as, to span a space or distance; to span a cylinder. NWAD SPAN.7
To measure. This soul doth span the world. NWAD SPAN.8
v.i. To agree in color, or in color and size; as, the horses span well. [New England.]
pert. of spin. We now use spun.
SNANCEL: n. A rope to tie a cow\'s hind legs.
SPANCEL: v.t. To tie the legs of a horse or cow with a rope .
SPANCOUNTER: n. A play at which within a span or circuit marked.
SPANFARTING: n. A play at which within a span or circuit marked.
SPANDREL: n. The space between the curve of an arch and the right lines inclosing it.
SPANG: n. A spangle or shining ornament; a thin piece of shining metal; something brilliant used as an ornament.
An y little thing sparkling and brilliant like pieces of metal; as crystals of ice. For the rich spangles that adorn the sky. NWAD SPANG.2
SPANGLE: v.t. To set or sprinkle with spangles; to adorn with small distinct brilliant bodies; as a spangled breastplate. What stars do spangle heaven with such beauty-
SPANGLING: ppr. Adorning with spangles. SPANIEL — SPECIAL_MATTER_IN_EVIDENCE
SPANIEL: A dog used in sports of the field, remarkable for his sagacity and obedience. NWAD SPANIEL.2
A mean, cringing, fawning person. NWAD SPANIEL.3
a. Like a spaniel; mean; fawning.
v.i. TO fawn; to cringe; to be obsequious.
v.t. To follow like a spaniel.
SPANISH-BROOM: n. A plant of the genus Spartium.
SPANISH-BROWN: n. A species of earth used in paints.
SPANISH-FLY: n. A fly or insect, the cantharis used in vesicatories, or composition for raising blisters.
SPANISH-WHITE: n. A white earth from Spain, used in paints.
SPANK: v.t. To strike with the open hand; to slap [A word common in New England.]
SPANKER: In seamen\'s language, a ship driver; a large sail occasionally set upon the mizenyard or gaff, the foot being extended by a boom. NWAD SPANKER.3
One that takes long strides in walking; also a stout person. NWAD SPANKER.4
SPANKING: Striking with the open hand NWAD SPANKING.2
SPAN-LONG: a. Of the length of a span.
SPANNER: The lock of a fusee or carbine; or the fusee itself. NWAD SPANNER.3
A wrench or nut screw-driver. NWAD SPANNER.4
SPANNING: ppr. Measuring with the hand; encompassing with the fingers.
SPAR: [If this word is connected with spare, the primary sense is probably thin. The sense of bar and spar, is however more generally derived from thrusting, shooting in length; so spear likewise. See Bar .]
A stone that breaks into a regular shape; marcasite. This name is popularly given to any crystalized mineral of a shining luster. NWAD SPAR.2
A round piece of timber. This name is usually given to the round pieces of timber used for the yards and top-masts of ships. NWAD SPAR.3
The bar of a gate. NWAD SPAR.4
v.t. To bar; to shut close or fasten with a bar.
v.i. [This is another form of the L. spiro. The primary sense is to urge, drive, throw, propel.]
To dispute; to quarrel in words; to wrangle. [This is the sense of the word in America.] NWAD SPAR.7
To fight with preclusive strokes. NWAD SPAR.8
SPARE: v.t. [It seems to be from the same root as L. parco.]
To use frugally; not to be profuse; not to waste. Thou thy Father\'s thunder did\'st not spare/ NWAD SPARE.2

To save or withhold from any particular use or occupation. He has no bread to spare, that is, to withhold from his necessary uses. All the time he could spare from the necessary cares of his weighty charge, he bestowed on prayer and serving of God. NWAD SPARE.3
To part with without much inconvenience; to do without. I could have better spar\'d a better man. Nor can we spare you long- NWAD SPARE.4
To omit; to forbear. We might have spared this toil and expense; Be pleas\'d your politics to spare. NWAD SPARE.5

To use tenderly; to treat with pity and forbearance; to forbear to afflict, punish or destroy. Spare us, good Lord. dim sadness did not spare celestial visages. But man alone can whom be conquers spare. NWAD SPARE.6
Not to take when in one\'s power; to forbear to destroy; as, to spare the life of a prisoner. NWAD SPARE.7
To grant; to allow; to indulge. Where anger Jove did never spare one breath of kind and temp\'rate air. NWAD SPARE.8
TO forbear to inflict of impose. Spare my sight the pain of seeing what a world of tears it cost you. NWAD SPARE.9
v.i.
TO live frugally; to be parsimonious. Who at some times spend, as other spare, divided between carelessness and care. NWAD SPARE.11
To forbear; to be scrupulous. To pluck and cat my fill I spar\'d not. NWAD SPARE.12
To be frugal; not to be profuse. NWAD SPARE.13
To use mercy or forbearance; to forgive to be tender. The king was sparing and compassionate towards hid subjects. NWAD SPARE.14
a.
Seanty; parsimonious; not abundant; as a spare diet. He was spare but discreet of speech. [We more generally use, in the latter application, sparing; as, he was sparing of words.] NWAD SPARE.16
That can be dispensed with; not wanted; superfluous. I have no spare time on my hands. If that no spare clothes he had to give. NWAD SPARE.17
Lean; wanting flesh; meager; thin. O give me your spare men and spare me the great ones. NWAD SPARE.18
Slow. [Not in use.] NWAD SPARE.19
n. Parsimony; frugal use. [Not in use.]
SPARENESS: n. State of being lean or thin; leanness.
SPARER: n. One that avoids unnecessary expense.
SPARERIB: n. [spare and rib.] The piece of a hog taken from the side, consisting of the ribs with little flesh on them.
SPARGEFACTION: n. [L. spargo, to sprinkle.] The act of sprinkling. [Not Used.]
SPARING: Using frugally; forbearing; omitting to punish or destroy. NWAD SPARING.2
Scanty; not plentiful; not abundant; as a sparing diet. NWAD SPARING.4
Saving; parsimonious. Virgil being so very sparing of his words, and leaving so much to be imagined by the reader, can never be translated as he ought in amy modern tongue. NWAD SPARING.5
SPARINGLY: Frugally; parsimoniously; not lavishly. High titles of honor were in the king\'s minority sparingly granted, because dignity then waited on desert. Commend but sparingly whom thou dost love. NWAD SPARINGLY.3
Abstinently; moderately. Christians are obliged to taste even the innocent pleasures of life but sparingly. NWAD SPARINGLY.4
Seldom; not frequently. The morality of a grave sentence, affected by Lucan, is more sparingly used by Virgil. NWAD SPARINGLY.5
SPARINGNESS: Parsimony; want of liberality. NWAD SPARINGNESS.2
SPARK: n. [The sense is that which shoots, darts off or scatters; probably allied to B. spargo.]
A small particle of fire or ignited substance, which is emitted from bodies in combustion, and which either ascends with the smoke, or is darted in another direction. NWAD SPARK.2
A small shining body or transient light. We have here and there a little clear light, and some sparks of bright knowledge. NWAD SPARK.3
A small portion of any thing active. If any spark of life is yet remaining. NWAD SPARK.4
A very small portion. If you have a spark or generosity. NWAD SPARK.5
A brisk, showy, gay man. The finest sparks and cleanest beaux. NWAD SPARK.6
v.i. To emit particles of fire; to sparkle. [Not in use.]
SPARKISH: Showy; well dressed; fine. NWAD SPARKISH.3
SPARKLE: To emit sparks; to send off small ignited particles; as burning fuel, etc. NWAD SPARKLE.5
To glitter; to glisten; as, a brilliant sparkles; sparkling colors. NWAD SPARKLE.6
To twinkle; to glitter; as sparkling stars. NWAD SPARKLE.7
To glisten; to exhibit an appearance of animation; as, the eyes sparkle with joy. NWAD SPARKLE.8
To emit little bubbles, as spirituous liquors; as sparkling wine. NWAD SPARKLE.9
v.i. To throw about; to scatter. [Not in use.]
SPARKLER: n. He or that which sparkles; one whose eyes sparkle.
SPARKLING: ppr. or a. Emitting sparks; glittering; lively; as sparkling wine; sparkling eyes.
SPARKLINGLY: adv. With twinkling or vivid brilliancy.
SPARROW: n. A small bird of the genus Fringilla and order of Passers. These birds are frequently seen about houses.
SPARROW-HAWK: n. A small species of short winged hawk.
SPARHAWK: n. A small species of short winged hawk.
SPARRY: a. [from spar.] Resembling spar, or consisting or spar; having a confused cyrstraline structure; spathose.
SPARSE: a. spars. [L. sparsus, scattered, from spargo.]
Thinly scattered; set or planted here and there; as a sparse population. NWAD SPARSE.2
In botany, not opposite, not alternate, nor in any apparent regular order; applied to branches, leaves peduncles, etc. NWAD SPARSE.3
v.t. spars. To disperse. [Not in use.]
SPARTAN: a. Pertaining to ancient Sparta; hence, hardly undaunted; as Spartan souls; Spartan bravery.
SPASM: n. [L. spasmus.] A n involuntary contraction of muscles or muscular fibers in animal bodies; irregular motion of the muscles or muscular fibers; convulsion; cramp.
SPASMODIC: a. Consisting in spasm; as a spasmodic affection.
n. A medicine good for removing spasm; but I believe the word generally employed in anti-spasmodic.
SPAT: pret. of spit, but nearly obsolete.
n. [from the root of spit; that which is ejected.]
The young of shell fish. NWAD SPAT.3
A petty combat; a little quarrel or dissension. [A vulgar use of the word in New England.] NWAD SPAT.4
SPATHACEOUS: a. Having a calyx like a sheath.
SPATHE: n. [L. spatha.] In botany, the calyx of a spadix opening or bursting longitudinally, in form of a sheath. It is also applied to the calyx of some flowers which have no spadix, as of narcissus, crocus, iris, etc.
SPATHIC: a. Foliated or lamellar. Spathic iron is a mineral of a foliated structure, and a yellowish or brownish color.
SPATHIFORM: a. [spath and form.] Resembling spar in form. The ocherous, spathiform and mineralized forms of urinate-
SPATHOUS: a. Having a calyx like a sheath.
SPATIATE: v.t. [L. spatior.] To rove; to ramble. [Not in use.]
SPATTER: v.t. [This root is a derivative of the family of spit, or L. pateo. See Sputter .]

To scatter a liquid substance on; to sprinkle with water or any fluid, or with any moist and dirty matter; as, to spatter a coat; to spatter the floor; to spatter the boots with mud. [This word, I believe, is applied always to fluid or moist substances. We say, to spatter with water, mud, blood or gravy; but never to spatter with dust or meal.] NWAD SPATTER.2
Figuratively, to asperse; to defame. [In this sense, asperse is generally used.] NWAD SPATTER.3
To throw out any thing offensive; as, to spatter foul speeches. [Not in use.] NWAD SPATTER.4
To scatter about; as, to spatter water here and there. NWAD SPATTER.5
v.i. To throw out of the mouth in a scattered manner; to sputter. [See Sputter .]
SPATTERDASHES: n. plu. [spatter and dash.] Coverings for the legs to keep them clean from water and mud. [Since boots are generally worn, these things and their name are little used.]
SPATTERED: Sprinkling with moist some liquid or dirty substance. NWAD SPATTERED.2
SPATTERING: Sprinkling with or foul matter. NWAD SPATTERING.2
SPATTLE: n. [L. spathula, spatha, a slice. from the root of L. pateo; so named from its breadth, or from its use in spreading things. A slice; an apothecaries\' instrument, for spreading plasters, etc.]
SPATTLING-POPPY: n. [L. papaver spumeum.] A plant; white behen; a species of Campion.
SPATULA: a. [from L. spathula.] In botany, a spatulate leaf is one shaped like a spatula or battledore, being roundish with a long, narrow, linear base; as in cistus incanus.
SPATULATE: a. [from L. spathula.] In botany, a spatulate leaf is one shaped like a spatula or battledore, being roundish with a long, narrow, linear base; as in cistus incanus.
SPAVIN: n. A tumor or excrescence that forms on the inside of a horse\'s hough, not far from the elbow; at first like gristle, but afterwards hard and bony.
SPAW: A mineral water from a place of this name in Germany. The name may perhaps be applied to other similar waters. NWAD SPAW.2
A spring of mineral water. NWAD SPAW.3
SPA: A mineral water from a place of this name in Germany. The name may perhaps be applied to other similar waters. NWAD SPAW.2
A spring of mineral water. NWAD SPAW.3
SPAWL: v.i. To throw saliva from the mouth in a scattering form; to disperse spittle in a careless dirty manner. Why must he sputter, spawl and slaver it?
n. Saliva or spittle thrown out carelessly.
SPAWLING: ppr. Throwing spittle carelessly from the mouth.
SPAWN: n. It has no plural. [If this word is not contracted, it belongs to the root of L. pano. If contracted, it probably belongs to the root of spew or spaw. The radical sense is that which is ejected or thrown out.]
The eggs of fish or frogs, when ejected. NWAD SPAWN.2
Any product or offspring; an expression of contempt. NWAD SPAWN.3
Offsets; shoots; suckers of plants. [Not in use in American.] NWAD SPAWN.4
To produce or deposit, as fishes do their eggs. NWAD SPAWN.6
To bring forth; to generate; in contempt. NWAD SPAWN.7
To deposit eggs, as fish or frogs. NWAD SPAWN.9
To issue, as offspring; in contempt. NWAD SPAWN.10
SPAWNED: pp. Produced or deposited, as the eggs of fish or frogs.
SPAWNER: n. the female fish. the spawner and the melter of the barbel cover their spawn with sand.
SPAY: v.t. [L. spado, a gelding.] To castrate the female of a beast by cutting and by taking out the uterus; as, to spay a sow.
SPAYED: pp. Castrated, as a female beast.
SPAYING: ppr. Castrating, as a female beast.
SPEAK: v.i. pret. spoke, [spake, nearly, Obs. ] pp. spoke, spoken. [It is easy to see that the root of this word is allied to that of beak peak, pick.]

To utter words or articulate sounds, as human beings; to express thoughts bywords. Children learn to speak at an early age. The organs may be so obstructed that a man may not be able to speak. Speak, Lord, for thy servant hearth. 1 Samuel 3:9 . NWAD SPEAK.2

To utter a speech, discourse or harangue; to utter thoughts in a public assembly. A man may be well informed on a subject, and yet to diffident to speak in public. Many of the nobility make them selves popular by speaking in parliament against those things which were most grateful to his majesty. NWAD SPEAK.3
To talk; to express opinions; to dispute. An honest man, sir, is able to speak for himself, when the knave is not. NWAD SPEAK.4
To discourse; to make mention of. Lucan speaks of a part of Cesar\'s army that came to him from the Leman lake. The Scripture speaks only of those to whom it speaks. NWAD SPEAK.5
To give sound. Make all your trumpets speak. NWAD SPEAK.6 To speak with, to converse with. Let me speak with my son. NWAD SPEAK.7

To utter with the mouth; to pronounce; to utter articulately; as human beings. They sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spoke a word to him. Job 2:13 . Speak the word, and my son shall be healed. Matthew 8:8 . NWAD SPEAK.9
To declare; to proclaim; to celebrate. It is my father\'s music to speak your deeds. NWAD SPEAK.10
To talk or converse in; to utter or pronounce, as in conversation. A man may know how to read and to understand a language which he cannot speak. NWAD SPEAK.11
To address; to accost. He will smile upon thee, put thee in hope, and speak thee fair. NWAD SPEAK.12
To exhibit; to make known. Let heav\'n\'s wide circuit speak the Maker\'s high magnificence. NWAD SPEAK.13
To express silently or by signs. The lady\'s looks or eyes speak the meaning or wishes of her heart. NWAD SPEAK.14

To communicate; as, to speak peace to the soul. NWAD SPEAK.15 To speak a ship, to hail and speak to her captain or commander. [Note. We say, to speak a word or syllable, to speak a sentence, an oration, piece, composition, or a dialogue, to speak a man\'s praise, etc.; but we never say, to speak an argument, a sermon or a story.] NWAD SPEAK.16
SPEAKABLE: That can be spoken. NWAD SPEAKABLE.2
Having the power of speech. NWAD SPEAKABLE.3
SPEAKER: n.
One that speaks, in what ever manner. NWAD SPEAKER.2
One that proclaims or celebrates. -No other speaker of my living actions. NWAD SPEAKER.3
One that utters or pronounces a discourse; usually, one that utters a speech in public. We say, a man is a good speaker, or a bad speaker. NWAD SPEAKER.4
The person who presides in a deliberative assembly, preserving order and regulating the debates; as the speaker of the house of commons; the speaker of a house or representatives. NWAD SPEAKER.5
SPEAKING: The act of uttering words; discourse. NWAD SPEAKING.3
In colleges, public declamation. NWAD SPEAKING.4
SPEAKING-TRUMPET: n. A trumpet by which the sound of the human voice may be propagated to a great distance.
SPEAR: A long pointed weapon, used in war and hunting by thrusting or throwing; a lance. NWAD SPEAR.2
A sharp pointed instrument with barbs; used for stabbing fish and other animals. NWAD SPEAR.3
A shoot, as of grass; usually spire. NWAD SPEAR.4
v.t. To pierce with a spear; to kill with a spear; as, to spear a fish.
v.i. To shoot into a long stem. [See Spire .]
SPEARED: pp. Pierced or killed with a spear.
SPEAR-FOOT: n. [spear and foot.] The far foot behind; used of a horse.
SPEAR-GRASS: A long stiff grass. NWAD SPEAR-GRASS.2
In New England, this name is given to a species of Poa. NWAD SPEAR-GRASS.3
SPEARING: Piercing or killing with a spear. NWAD SPEARING.2
Shooting into a long stem. NWAD SPEARING.3
SPEARMAN: n. [spear and man.] One who is armed with a spear. Psalm 68:30 .
SPEARMINT: n. [spear and mint.] A plant of the genus Mentha; a species of mint.
SPEAR-THISTLE: n. A plant, a troublesome weed.
SPEAR-WORT: n. A plant; the popular name of the Ranunculus flammula.
SPECHT: n. A wood pecker. [Not in use.]
SPEIGHT: n. A wood pecker. [Not in use.]
SPECIAL: a. [from L. specialis, from species, form, figure, sort, from specio, to see. Hence species primarily is appearance, that which is presented to the eye. This word and especial are the same.]
Designating a species of sort. A special idea is called by the schools a species. NWAD SPECIAL.2

Particular; peculiar; noting something more than ordinary. She smiles with a special grace. Our Savior is represented every where in Scripture as the special patron of the poor and afflicted. NWAD SPECIAL.3
Appropriate; designed for a particular purpose. A private grant is made by a special act of parliament or of congress. NWAD SPECIAL.4
Extraordinary; uncommon. Our charities should be universal, but chiefly exercised on special opportunities. NWAD SPECIAL.5
Chief in excellence. The king hath drawn the special head of all the land together. NWAD SPECIAL.6
SPECIAL ADMINISTRATION: in law, is one in which the power of an administrator is limited to the administration of certain specific effects, and not the effects in general of the deceased.
SPECIAL BAIL: consists of actual sureties recognized to answer for the appearance of person in court; as distinguished from common boil, which is nominal.
SPECIAL BAILIF: is a bailif appointed by the sherif for making arrests and serving processes.
SPECIAL DEMURRER: is one in which the cause of demurrer is particularly stated.
SPECIAL IMPARLANCE: is one in which there is a saving of all exceptions to the writ or count, or of all exception whatsoever.
SPECIAL JURY: is one which is called upon motion of either party, when the cause is supposed to require it.
SPECIAL MATTER IN EVIDENCE: the particular facts in the case on which the defendant relies. SPECIAL_PLEA — SPERICALNESS
SPECIAL PLEA: in bar, is a plea which sets forth the particular facts or reasons why the plaintif\'s demand should be barred as a release, accord, etc.
SPECIAL PROPERTY: a qualified or limited property, as the property which a man acquires in wild animals by reclaiming them.
SPECIAL SESSION OF A COURT: an extraordinary session; a session beyond the regular stated sessions; or in corporations and counties in England, a petty session held by a few justices for dispatching small business.
SPECIAL STATUE: is a private act of the legislature, such as respects a private act of the legislature, such as respect a private person or individual.
SPECIAL TAIL: is where a gift is restrained to certain hears of the donee\'s body, and does not descend to the heirs in general.
SPECIAL VERDICT: is a verdict in which the jury find the facts and state them as proved, but leave the law arising from the facts to be determined by the court. Another method of finding a special verdict, is when the jury find a verdict generally for the plaintif, but subject to the opinion of the court on a special case stated by the counsel on both sides, with regard to a matter of law.
SPECIAL WARRENT: a warrant to take a person and bring him before a particular justice who granted the warrant.
SPECIALIZE: v.t. To mention specially. [Not in use.]
SPECIALLY: Particularly; in a manner beyond what is common, or out of the ordinary course. Every signal deliverance form danger ought to be specially noticed as a divine interposition. NWAD SPECIALLY.2
For a particular purpose. A meeting of the legislature is specially summoned. NWAD SPECIALLY.3
SPECIALTY: Particularity. specialty of rule hat been neglected. NWAD SPECIALTY.2
A particular or peculiar case. Note. This word is now little used in the senses above. Its common acceptation is, NWAD SPECIALTY.3
A special contract; an obligation or bond; the evidence of a debt by deed or instrument under seal. Such a debt is called a debt by specialty, in distinction from simple contract. NWAD SPECIALTY.4
SPECIE: n. spe\'shy. Coin; copper, silver or gold coined and used as a circulating medium of commerce. [See Special .]
SPECIES: n. spe\'shiz. [L. from specio, to see. See Special .]

In zoology, a collection of organized beings derived from one common parentage by natural generation, characterized by one peculiar from one common parentage by natural generation, characterized by one peculiar form, liable to vary within certain narrow limits. These accidental and limited variations are varieties. Different races from the same parents are called varieties. NWAD SPECIES.2

In botany, all the plants which spring from the same see, or which resemble each other in certain character or in variable forms. There are as many species as there are different in variable forms or circumstances only with in certain narrow limits. These accidental and limited variations are varieties. Different races from the same parents are called varieties. NWAD SPECIES.3
In logic, a special idea, corresponding to the specific distinctions of things in nature. NWAD SPECIES.4
Sort; kind; in a loose sense; as a species of low cunning in the world; as a species of generosity; a species of cloth. NWAD SPECIES.5

Appearance to the senses; visible or sensible representation. An apparent diversity between the species visible and audible, is that the visible doth not mingle in the medium, but the audible doth. The species of letters illuminated with indigo and violet. [Little used.] NWAD SPECIES.6

Representation to the min. Wit-the faculty of imagination in the writer, which searches over all the memory for the species or ideas of those things which it designs to present. [Little used.] NWAD SPECIES.7
Show; visible exhibition. Shows and species serve best with the common people. [Not in use.] NWAD SPECIES.8

Coin, or coined silver and gold, used as a circulating medium; as the current species of Europe. In modern practice. this word is contracted into specie. What quantity of specie has the bank in its vault? What is the amount of all the current specie in the country? What is the value in specie, of a bill of exchange? We receive payment for goods in specie, not in bank notes. NWAD SPECIES.9
In pharmacy, a simple; a component part of a compound medicine. NWAD SPECIES.10 10. The old pharmaceutical term for powders. NWAD SPECIES.11
SPECIFIC: n. In medicine, a remedy that certainly cures particular disease.

That makes a thing of the species of which it is designating the peculiar property of properties of a thing, which constitute its species, and distinguish it from other things. Thus we say, the specific form of an animal or a plant; the specific form of a cube or square; the specific qualities of a plant or a drug; the specific difference between an acid and an alkali; the specific distinction between virtue and vice. Specific difference is that primary attribute which distinguishes each species form one another. NWAD SPECIFIC.2

In medicine, appropriate for the cure of a particular disease; that certainly cures or is less fallible than others; as a specific remedy for the gout. The Saratogs waters are found to be a specific remedy, or nearly so, for the cure of bilious complaints, so called. NWAD SPECIFIC.3
SPECIFICAL: That makes a thing of the species of which it is designating the peculiar property of properties of a thing, which constitute its species, and distinguish it from other things. Thus we say, the specific form of an animal or a plant; the specific form of a cube or square; the specific qualities of a plant or a drug; the specific difference between an acid and an alkali; the specific distinction between virtue and vice. Specific difference is that primary attribute which distinguishes each species form one another. NWAD SPECIFIC.2

In medicine, appropriate for the cure of a particular disease; that certainly cures or is less fallible than others; as a specific remedy for the gout. The Saratogs waters are found to be a specific remedy, or nearly so, for the cure of bilious complaints, so called. NWAD SPECIFIC.3
SPECIFIC CHARACTER: in botany, a circumstance or circumstances distinguishing one species from every other species of the same genus.
SPECIFIC GRAVITY: in philosophy, the weight that belongs to an equal bulk of each body. [See Gravity .]
SPECIFIC NAME: in botany, is the trivial name as distinguished form the generic na, e. Specific name is now used for the name which, appended to the name of the genus, constitutes the distinctive name of the species; but it was originally applied by Linne to the essential character of the species, or the essential difference. The present specific names he at fist called the trivial names.
SPECIFICALLY: adv. In such a manner as to constitute a species; according to the nature of the species. A body is specifically lighter than another, when it has less weight in the same bulk than the other. Human reason-differs specifically from the fantastic reason of brutes. -Those several virtues that are specifically requisite to a due performance of duty.
SPECIFICATION: The act of determining by a mark or limit; notation of limits. The specification of limitation of the question hinders the disputers from wandering away from the precise point of inquiry. NWAD SPECIFICATION.2
The act of specifying; designation of particulars; particular mention; as the specification of a charge against a military or naval officer. NWAD SPECIFICATION.3
Article or thing specified. NWAD SPECIFICATION.4
SPECIFY: v.t. To mention or name, as a particular thing; to designate in words so as to distinguish a thing from every other; as, to specify the uses of a plant; to specify the articles one wants to purchase. He has there given us an exact geography of Greece, where the countries and the uses of their soils are specified.
SPECIMEN: n. [L. from species, with the termination men, which corresponds in sense to the English hood or ness.] A sample; a part or small portion of any thing, intended to exhibit the kind and quality of the whole, or of something not exhibited; as a specimen of a man\'s handwriting; a specimen of painting or composition; specimen of one\'s art or skill.
SPECIOUS: Showy; pleasing to the view. The rest, far greater part will deem in outward rites and specious form religion satisfied. NWAD SPECIOUS.2

Apparently right; superficially fair, just or correct\' plausible; appearing well at first view; as specious reasoning; a specious argument; a specious objection; specious deeds. Temptation is of greater danger, because it is covered with the specious names of good nature, good manners, nobleness of mind, etc. NWAD SPECIOUS.3
SPECIOUSLY: adv. With a fair appearance; with show of right; as, to reason speciously.
SPECK: n. [This word may be formed from peck, for peckled has been used for speckled, spotted as though pecked.]
A spot; a stain; a small place in any thing that is discolored by foreign matter, or is of a color different from that of the main substance; as a speck on paper or cloth. NWAD SPECK.2
A very small thing. NWAD SPECK.3
v.t. To spot; to stain in spots or drops.
SPECKLE: n. A little spot in any thing, of a different substance or color from that of the thing itself.
v.t. To mark with small spots of a different color; used chiefly in the participle passive, which see.
SPECKLED: pp. or a. Marked with specks; variegated with spots of a different color from the ground or surface of the object; as the speckled breast of a bird; a speckled serpent.
SPECKLED BIRD: a denomination given to a person of doubtful character or principles.
SPECKLEDNESS: n. The state of being speckled.
SPECKTACLE: n. [L. spectaculum, from specto, to behold; specio, to see.]

A show; something exhibited to view; usually, something presented to view as extraordinary, or something that is beheld as unusual and worthy of special notice. Thus we call things exhibited for amusement, public spectacles, as the combats of gladiators in ancient Rome. We are made a spectacle to the world, and to angels, and to men. 1 Corinthians 4:9 . NWAD SPECKTACLE.2
Any thing seen; a sight. A drunkard is a shocking spectacle. NWAD SPECKTACLE.3
Spectacles, in the plural, glasses to assist the sight. NWAD SPECKTACLE.4
Figuratively, something that aids the intellectual sight. Shakespeare needed not the spectacles of books to read nature. NWAD SPECKTACLE.5
SPECTATOR: One that looks on; one that sees or beholds; a beholder; as the spectators of the show. NWAD SPECTATOR.2
One personally present. The spectators were numerous. NWAD SPECTATOR.3
SPECTATORSHIP: The act of beholding. NWAD SPECTATORSHIP.2
The office or quality of a spectator. NWAD SPECTATORSHIP.3
SPECTATRESS: n. [L. spectatrix.] A female beholder or looker on.
SPECTATRIX: n. [L. spectatrix.] A female beholder or looker on.
SPECTER: n. [L. spectrum, from specto, to behold.]
An apparition; the appearance of a person who is dead; a ghost. The ghosts of traitors from the bridge descend, With bold fanatic specters to rejoice. NWAD SPECTER.2
Something made preternaturally visible. NWAD SPECTER.3
In conchology, a species of voluta, marked with reddish broad bands. NWAD SPECTER.4
SPECTRUM: n. [L.] A visible form; an image of something seen, continuing after image of something seen, continuing after the eyes are closed, covered or turned away. This is called an ocular spectrum.
SPECULAR: a. [L. specularis, from speculum, a mirror, from specio, to see.]
Having the qualities of a mirror or looking glass; having a smooth reflecting surface; as a specular metal; a specular surface. NWAD SPECULAR.2
Assisting sight. [Improper and not used.] NWAD SPECULAR.3
SPECULATE: v.i. [L. speculor, to view, to contemplate, from specio, to see.]

To meditate; to contemplate; to consider a subject by turning it in the mind and viewing it in its different aspects and relations; as, to speculate on political events; to speculate on the probable results of a discovery. NWAD SPECULATE.2

In commerce, to purchase land, goods, stock or other things, with the expectation of an advance in price, and of selling the articles with a profit by means of such advance; as, to speculate in coffee, or in sugar, or in six percent stock, or in bank stock. NWAD SPECULATE.3
v.t. To consider attentively; as, to speculate the nature of a thing. [Not in use.]
SPECUATION: Examination by the eye; view [Little used.] NWAD SPECUATION.2

Mental view of any thing in its various aspects and relations; contemplation; intellectual examination. The events of the day afford matter of serious speculation to the friends of christianity. Thenceforth to speculations high or deep. I turn\'d my thoughts- NWAD SPECUATION.3
Train of thoughts formed by meditation. From him Socrates derived the principles of morality and most part of his natural speculations. NWAD SPECUATION.4

Mental scheme; theory; views of a subject not verified by fact or practice. This globe, which was formerly round only in speculation, has been circumnavigated. The application of steam to navigation is no longer a matter of mere speculation. Speculations which originate in guilt, must end in ruin. NWAD SPECUATION.5
Power of sight. Thou hast no speculation in those eyes. [Not in use.] NWAD SPECUATION.6

In commerce, the act or practice of buying land or goods, etc. in expectation of a rise as distinguished from a regular trade, in which the profit expected is the difference between the retail and wholesale prices, or the difference of price in the place where the good are purchased, and the place to which they are to be carried for market. In England, France and America, public stock is the subject of continual speculation. In the United States, a few men have been enriched, but many have been ruined by speculation. NWAD SPECUATION.7
SPECULATIST: n. One who speculates or forms theories; a speculator.
SPECULATIVE: Given to speculation; contemplative; applied to persons. The min of man being by nature speculative- NWAD SPECULATIVE.2
Formed by speculation; theoretical; ideal; not verified by fact, experiment or practice; as a scheme merely speculative. NWAD SPECULATIVE.3
Pertaining to view; also, prying. NWAD SPECULATIVE.4
SPECULATIVELY: In contemplation; with meditation. NWAD SPECULATIVELY.2
Ideally; theoretically; in theory only, not in practice. Propositions seem often to be speculatively true, which experience does not verify. NWAD SPECULATIVELY.3
SPECULATIVENESS: n. The state of being speculative, or of consisting in speculation only.
SPECULATOR: One who speculates or forms theories. NWAD SPECULATOR.2
An observer; a contemplator. NWAD SPECULATOR.3
A spy; a watcher. NWAD SPECULATOR.4
In commerce, one who buys goods, land or other thing, with the expectation of a rise of price, and of deriving profit from such advance. NWAD SPECULATOR.5
SPECULATORY: Intended or adapted for viewing or espying. NWAD SPECULATORY.3
SPECULM: A mirror or looking glass. NWAD SPECULM.2
A glass that reflects the images of objects. NWAD SPECULM.3
A metallic reflector used in catadioptric telescopes. NWAD SPECULM.4
In surgery, an instrument for dilating and keeping open certain parts of the body. NWAD SPECULM.5
SPEECH: The faculty of uttering articulate sounds or words, as in human beings; the faculty of expressing thoughts by words or articulate sounds. Speech was given to man by his Creator for the noblest purposes. NWAD SPEECH.2
Language; words as expressing ideas. The acts of God to human ears cannot without process of speech be told. NWAD SPEECH.3
A particular language, as distinct form others. Psalm 19:3 . NWAD SPEECH.4
That which is spoken; words uttered in connection and expressing thoughts. You smile at my speech. NWAD SPEECH.5
Talk; mention; common saying. The duke did of me demand, what was the speech among the londoners concerning the French journey. NWAD SPEECH.6
Formal discourse in public; oration; harangue. The member has made his first speech in the legislature. NWAD SPEECH.7
Any declaration of thoughts. I, with leave of speech implor\'d, repli\'d. NWAD SPEECH.8
v.i. To make a speech; to harangue. [Little used.]
SPEECHLESS: Destitute or deprived of the faculty of speech. More generally, NWAD SPEECHLESS.2
Mute; silent; not speaking for a time. Speechless with wonder, and half dead with fear. NWAD SPEECHLESS.3
SPEECHLESSNESS: n. The state of being speechless; muteness.
SPEECH-MAKER: n. One who makes speeches; one who speaks much in a public assembly.
SPEED: v.i. pret. and pp. sped, speeded. [The L. expedio may be from the same root, which signifies to drive, to hurry, of the family of L. peto.]
To make haste; to move with celerity. NWAD SPEED.2

To have success; to prosper; to succeed; that is, to advance in one\'s enterprise. He that\'s once demi\'d will hardly speed. Those that profaned and abused the second temple, sped no better. NWAD SPEED.3
To have any condition good or ill; to fare. Ships heretofore in seas like fishes sped, The mightiest still upon the smallest fed. NWAD SPEED.4
TO dispatch; to send away in haste. He sped him thence home to his habitation. NWAD SPEED.6
To hasten; to hurry; to put in quick motion. -But sped his steps along the hoarse resounding shore. NWAD SPEED.7
TO hasten to a conclusion; to execute; to dispatch; as, to speed judicial acts. NWAD SPEED.8
To assist; to help forward; to hasten. -With rising gales that sped their happy flight. NWAD SPEED.9
To prosper; to cause to succeed. May heaven speed this undertaking. NWAD SPEED.10
To furnish in haste. NWAD SPEED.11

To dispatch; to kill; to ruin; to destroy. With a speeding thrust his heart he found. A dire dilemma! either way I\'m sped; If foes, they write if friends they read me dead. NWAD SPEED.12 Note In the phrase, “God speed,” there is probably a gross mistake in considering it as equivalent to “may God give you success.” The true phrase is probably “good speed; good, in Saxon, being written god. I bid you or wish you good speed, that is, good success. NWAD SPEED.13

Swiftness; quickness; celerity; applied to animals. We say, a man or a horse runs or travels with speed; a fowl flies with speed. We speak of the speed of a fish in the water, but we do not speak of the speed of a river, or of wind, or of a falling body. I think however I have seen the word applied to the lapse of time and the motion of lightning, but in poetry only. NWAD SPEED.15
Haste; dispatch; as, to perform a journey with speed; to execute an order with speed. NWAD SPEED.16
Rapid pace; as a horse of speed. We say also, high speed, full speed. NWAD SPEED.17

Success; prosperity in an undertaking; favorable issue; that is, advance to the desired end. O Lord God of my master Abraham, I pray thee, send me good speed this day. Genesis 24:12 . This use is retained in the proverb, “to make more haste than good speed,” and in the Scriptural phrase, “to bid one good speed,” [Not God speed, as erroneously written.] NWAD SPEED.18
SPEEDILY: adv. Quickly; with haste; in a short time. Send speedily to Bertram.
SPEEDINESS: n. The quality of being speedy; quickness; celerity; haste; dispatch.
SPEEDWELL: n. A plant of the genus Veronica.
SPEEDY: Quick; swift; nimble; hasty; rapid in motion; as a speedy flight; on speedy foot. NWAD SPEEDY.2
Quick in performance; not dilatory or slow; as a speedy dispatch of business. NWAD SPEEDY.3
SPEET: v.t. [from the root of spit.] To stab. [Not in use.]
SPELK: n. A splinter; a small stick or rod used in thatching.
SPELL: n. [The verb primarily signifies to throw or drive, and is probably formed on the root of L. pello. In some of the application of spell, we observe the sense of turn. We observe the same in throw, warp, cant, etc.]
A story; a tale. NWAD SPELL.2
A charm consisting of some words of occult power. Start not; her actions shall be holy; you hear my speel is lawful. Begin, begin; the mystic spell prepare. NWAD SPELL.3
A turn of work; relief; turn of duty. Take a spell at the pump. Their toil is so extreme, that they cannot endure it above four hours in a day, but are succeed by spells. NWAD SPELL.4
In New England, a short time; a little time. [Not elegant.] NWAD SPELL.5
A turn of gratuitous labor, sometimes accompanied with presents. People give their neighbors a spell. NWAD SPELL.6
v.t. pret. and pp. spelled or spelt.

To tell or name the letters of a word, with a proper division of syllables, for the with a proper division of syllables, for the purpose of learning the pronunciation. In this matter children learn to read by first spelling the words. NWAD SPELL.8
To write or print with the proper letters; to form words by correct orthography. The word satire ought to be spelled with i, and not with y. NWAD SPELL.9
To take another\'s place or turn temporarily in any labor or service. [This is a popular use of the word in New England.] NWAD SPELL.10
To charm; as spelled with words of power. NWAD SPELL.11
To read; to discover by characters or marks; with out; as, to speel out the sense of an author. We are not left to spell out a God in the works of creation. NWAD SPELL.12
To tell; to relate; to teach. [Not in use.] NWAD SPELL.13
To form words with the proper letters, either in reading or writing. He knows not how to spell. Our orthography is so irregular that most persons never learn to spell. NWAD SPELL.15
SPELLED: n. One that spells; one skilled in spelling.
SPELLER: n. One that spells; one skilled in spelling.
SPELLING: Naming the letters of a word, or writing them; forming words with their proper letters. NWAD SPELLING.2
The act of naming the letters of a word, or the act of writing or printing words with their proper letters. NWAD SPELLING.5
Orthography; the manner of forming words with letters. Bad spelling is disreputable to a gentleman. NWAD SPELLING.6
SPELLING-BOOK: n. A book for teaching children to spell and read.
SPELTER: n. Common zink, which contains a portion of lead, copper, iron, a little arsenic, manganese and plumbago.
SPENCE: n. spens. A buttery; a larder; a place where provisions are kept.
SPENCER: One who has the care of the spence or buttery. NWAD SPENCER.2
A kind of short coat. NWAD SPENCER.3
SPEND: v.t. pret. and pp. spent. [L. expendo; from the root of L. pando, pendeo, the primary sense of which is to strain, to open or spread; allied to span, pane, etc.]
To lay out; to dispose of; to part with; as, to spend money for clothing. Why do ye spend money for that which is not bread? Isaiah 55:2 . NWAD SPEND.2
To consume; to waste; to squander; as to spend an estate in gaming or other vices. NWAD SPEND.3
To consume; to exhaust. The provisions were spent, and the troops were in want. NWAD SPEND.4
To bestow for any purpose; often with on or upon. It is folly to spend words in debate on trifles. NWAD SPEND.5
To pass, as time; to suffer to pass away. They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment go down to the grave. Job 21:13 . NWAD SPEND.7
To lay out; to exert or to waste; to wear away; as, to spend one\'s strength. NWAD SPEND.8
To exhaust of force; to waste; to wear away; as, a ball had spend its force. The violence of the waves was spent. Heaps of spent arrows fall and strew the ground. NWAD SPEND.9
To exhaust of strength; to harass; to fatigue. Their bodies spent with long labor and thirst- NWAD SPEND.10
To make expense; to make disposition of money. He spends like a prudent man. NWAD SPEND.12
To be lost or wasted; to vanish; to be dissipated. The sound spendeth and is dissipated in the open air. NWAD SPEND.13
To prove in the use. -Butter spent as if it cam from the richer soil. NWAD SPEND.14
To be consumed. Candles spend fast in a current of air Our provision spend rapidly. NWAD SPEND.15
To be employed to any use. The vines they use for wine are so often cut, that their sap spendeth into the grapes. [Unusual.] NWAD SPEND.16
SPENDER: n. One that spends; also, a prodigal; a lavisher.
SPENDING: ppr. Laying out; consuming; wasting; exhausting.
SPENDTHRIFT: n. [spend and thrift.] One who spends money profusely or improvidently; a prodigal; one who lavishes his estate.
SPERABLE: a. [L. sperabilis, from spero, to hope.] That may be hoped. [Not in use.]
SPERM: Animal seed; that by which the species is propagated. NWAD SPERM.2

The head matter of a certain species of whale, called cachalot. It is called by the French blanc de baleine, the white of whales. It is found also in other parts of the body; but it is improperly named, not being a spermatic substance. Of this matter are mad candles of a beautiful white color. NWAD SPERM.3
Spawn of fishes or frogs. NWAD SPERM.4
SPERMACETO: n. [L. sperma, sperm, and cetus, a whale. It is pronounced as it is written.] The same as sperm.
SPERMATIC: Consisting of seed; seminal. NWAD SPERMATIC.2
Pertaining to the semen, or conveying it; as spermatic vessels. NWAD SPERMATIC.3
SPERMATIZE: v.i. To yield seed. [Not in use.]
SPERMATOCELE: n. A swelling of the spermatic vessels, or vessels of the testicles.
SPET: v.t. To spit; to throw out. [Not in use.]
n. Spittle, or a flow. [Not in use.]
SPEW: v.i. To vomit; to discharge the contents of the stomach.
To vomit; to puke; to eject from the stomach. NWAD SPEW.2
To eject; to cast forth. NWAD SPEW.3
To cast out with abhorrence. Leviticus 18:28 . NWAD SPEW.4
SPUE: To vomit; to puke; to eject from the stomach. NWAD SPEW.2
To eject; to cast forth. NWAD SPEW.3
To cast out with abhorrence. Leviticus 18:28 . NWAD SPEW.4
SPEWING: ppr. Vomiting; ejecting from the stomach.
SPHACELATE: To mortify; to become gangrenous; as flesh. NWAD SPHACELATE.2
To decay or become carious, as a bone. NWAD SPHACELATE.3
SPHACLATION: n. The process of becoming or making gangrenous; mortification.
SPHACELUS: In medicine and surgery, gangrene; mortification of the flesh of a living animal. NWAD SPHACELUS.2
Caries or decay of a bone. NWAD SPHACELUS.3
SPHAGNOUS: a. [shagnum, bog-moss. Linne.] Pertaining to bog-moss; mossy.
SPHENE: n. A mineral composed of nearly equal parts of oxyd of titanium, silex and lime. Its colors are commonly grayish, yellowish, redish and blackish brown, and various shades of green. It is found amorphous and in crystals.
SPHENOID: a. Resembling a wedge. The spenoid bone, is the pterygoid bone of the basis of the skull.
SPHENOIDAL: a. Resembling a wedge. The spenoid bone, is the pterygoid bone of the basis of the skull.
SPHERE: In geometry, a solid body contained under a single surface, which in every part is equally distant from a point called its center. The earth is not an exact sphere. The sun appears to be a sphere. NWAD SPHERE.2
An orb or globe of the mundane system. First the sun, a mighty sphere, he fram\'d. Then mortal ears had heard the music of the spheres. NWAD SPHERE.3
An orbicular body, or a circular figure representing the earth or apparent heavens. NWAD SPHERE.4
Circuit of motion; revolution; orbit; as the diurnal sphere. NWAD SPHERE.5
The concave or vast orbicular expanse in which the heavenly orbs appear. NWAD SPHERE.6

Circuit of action, knowledge or influence; compass; province; employment. Every man has his particular sphere of action, in which it should be his ambition to excel. Events of this kind have repeatedly fallen within the sphere of my knowledge. This man treats of matters not within his sphere. NWAD SPHERE.7

Rank; order of society. Persons moving in a higher sphere claim more deference. NWAD SPHERE.8 Sphere Of Activity of a body, the whole space or extent reached by the effluvia emitted from it. NWAD SPHERE.9 A Right Sphere, that aspect of the heavens in which the circles of daily motion of the heavenly bodies, are perpendicular to the horizon. A spectator at the equator views a right sphere. NWAD SPHERE.10 A Parallel Sphere, that in which the circles of daily motion are parallel to the horizon. A spectator at either of the poles, would view a parallel sphere. NWAD SPHERE.11 An Oblique Sphere, that in which the circles of daily motion are oblique to the horizon. as is the case to a spectator at any point between the equator and either pole. NWAD SPHERE.12 Armillary Sphere, an artificial representation of the circles of the sphere, by means of brass rings. NWAD SPHERE.13
To place in a sphere. The glorious planet Sol in novel eminence enthron\'d, and spher\'d amidst the res. [Unusual.] NWAD SPHERE.15
To form into roundness; as light sphered in a radiant cloud. NWAD SPHERE.16
SPHERIC: Globular; orbicular; having a surface in every part equally distant from the center; as a spherical body. Drops of water take a spherical form. NWAD SPHERIC.2

Planetary; relating to the orbs of the planets. We make guilty of our disasters the sun, the moon and the stars, as if we were villains by spherical predominance. NWAD SPHERIC.3 Spherical Geometry. that branch of geometry which teats of spherical magnitudes. NWAD SPHERIC.4 Spherical Triangle, a triangle formed by the mutual intersection of three great circles of the sphere. NWAD SPHERIC.5 Spherical Trigonometry, that branch of trigonometry which teaches to compute the sides and angles of spherical triangles. NWAD SPHERIC.6
SPHERICAL: Globular; orbicular; having a surface in every part equally distant from the center; as a spherical body. Drops of water take a spherical form. NWAD SPHERIC.2

Planetary; relating to the orbs of the planets. We make guilty of our disasters the sun, the moon and the stars, as if we were villains by spherical predominance.
